newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Busang seen haunting Indonesia despite potential.
newsitem.headline: Busang seen haunting Indonesia despite potential.

text.p: Indonesia will remain a magnet for mineral prospectors despite the Busang scandal, but the ghost of the biggest mining fraud in history will haunt the country for years to come, industry officials said on Wednesday.

"The geology of Indonesia doesn't change (because of Busang). For foreign companies, Indonesia is still a good place to carry out exploration," Beni Wahju, president-director of PT Ingold Management, told Reuters.
Ingold is 80-percent owned by giant nickel miner Inco Ltd of Canada, with former Indonesian mines minister Mohammad Sadli holding the remaining 20 percent.

"It will continue to be a good place to carry out exploration work as long as it continues to honour contracts of work," Wahju said, referring to written government approval needed to explore for and mine minerals across Indonesia.
Other industry officials said, however, the fallout from the Busang debacle would be evident when the government approves its next batch of contracts of work (COW).
They said some 160 foreign mining companies had applied for the so-called seventh generation COW, which were currently being processed by the government.

"Nearly half of the companies which have applied for the seventh-generation COW are junior exploration companies," one industry official said. "Many of them will be unable to raise funds for exploration because of what happened in Busang."

The Busang discovery -- touted by Canadian exploration company Bre-X Minerals Ltd as the biggest gold find this century -- collapsed under the weight of an independent audit that found no economic gold deposit on the property.
Mining consultant Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd's report also said data to which the discovery was pegged was falsified on a scale "without precedent in the history of mining".
The Indonesian government has temporarily closed down all activities of Bre-X and its subsidiaries working in the archipelago pending an investigation.
The government has also said it was planning to tighten mining regulations, including asking foreign mining firms to allocate a 10-percent stake in all future projects.

Busang collapsed as Bre-X's partners, Freeport McMoRan Copper and Gold Inc, the Nusamba Group that is linked to President Suharto and the Indonesian government withdrew from the project, once said to be worth about $24 billion.

Mining engineer M. Simatupang of the Indonesia Mining Association said on Wednesday Indonesia offered vast exploration opportunities from Sumatra island to the far reaches of Irian Jaya province, the site of a world-class copper and gold mine.
"There might not be another Busang, but there is plenty of exploration potential in Indonesia," he said. "In my 40 years in the business, I have not seen anything like Busang."

Industry officials said as investigations into Busang began, the spotlight was shifting to the Indonesian government's bid to secure a stake in the Batu Hijau copper and gold project, 80 percent owned by U.S. Newmont Mining Corp.
"I am more concerned about Newmont than Busang," one official said. "The Newmont contract should be honoured."
Mines Minister Ida Bagus Sudjana said on Tuesday the government was seeking a 10-percent stake in the project, but Newmont rejected the move on Wednesday saying it was not feasible.

Batu Hijau, located in West Nusa Tenggara province and which would cost $2 billion to develop, contains an estimated 5.3 million tonnes of copper and 13.4 million ounces of gold. The project has received a COW but is awaiting government approval to begin construction of a mine.
